issues.legal_issue: Demolition of a building after a show-cause process is unlawful when the affected person is not given the required further notice before demolition.
material_facts: The municipal authorities issued show-cause notices and proceeded to demolish the structures without giving the affected persons the further notice required before demolition.
The applicable statutory amendment fixed the time for replying to a show-cause notice but did not displace the earlier direction requiring a further notice before demolition.
issues.conclusion: The demolitions carried out without the further notice were unlawful. For existing buildings, the authority must consider any reply, issue a reasoned order if the reply is unsatisfactory, and give a further notice before demolition; a separate procedure applies to ongoing construction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 351(1A) of the Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act sets the show-cause procedure and reply period, while Section 351(2) authorizes removal if sufficient cause is not shown. The court applied Sopan Maruti Thopte v. Pune Municipal Corporation, holding that its further-notice direction remained in force because the amendment changed the initial reply period but did not alter the period before demolition. The court also set out procedures distinguishing existing buildings from ongoing construction, including reasoned decisions and further notice after an unsatisfactory reply.

predicates.municipal_demolition_proceeding: A municipal authority is taking action to demolish a building or structure.
predicates.demolition_without_further_notice: The authority demolishes the structure without giving the affected person the further notice required after the show-cause process.

issues.definition: When a municipal demolition proceeding results in demolition without the required further notice, the demolition procedure is unlawful.

issues.legal_issue: A procedural defect in demolition does not by itself justify an order permitting the demolished structure to be rebuilt.
material_facts: The structures had been demolished without compliance with the required notice procedure.
The High Court permitted reconstruction without finding that the structures were lawful; the legality of the structures was not established in those proceedings.
In one appeal the structure had already been rebuilt, while in the other reconstruction had not taken place.
issues.conclusion: An illegal structure cannot be permitted to be re-erected even if its demolition was procedurally unlawful. Reconstruction may be permitted only after a clear finding that the original structure was lawful and the permitted structure is sufficiently identified, or construction may proceed in accordance with applicable by-laws and requisite permissions. Compensation may be awarded for unlawful demolition, with recovery from officials who acted unlawfully. The already rebuilt structure was not undone, but fresh lawful proceedings were directed; the order permitting reconstruction in the other appeal was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The court balanced procedural fairness and private rights against the rule of law and the public interest in preventing illegal and unplanned construction. It relied on the principles discussed in Sopan Maruti Thopte v. Pune Municipal Corporation, while holding that procedural illegality does not validate an illegal structure or justify perpetuating illegality. Where a structure is found lawful, any reconstruction order must identify the structure with sufficient specificity; alternatively, construction may be undertaken under existing by-laws and permissions.

predicates.writ_reconstruction_claim: A person asks a writ court to permit reconstruction of a structure demolished by a public authority.
predicates.demolition_procedure_unlawful: The public authority demolished the structure without following the required procedure.

issues.definition: If reconstruction is sought after procedurally unlawful demolition, it requires a clear finding that the structure was lawful and a defined reconstruction, or construction under applicable requirements.

issues.legal_issue: Large municipal corporations in the State must use geomapping and geo-photography to document their areas and newly incorporated areas.
material_facts: The court was informed that disputes arise about the dimensions and nature of structures, particularly in areas later brought within municipal boundaries, and that some structures lack sanctioned plans.
The court considered geomapping, satellite imagery, drones, and vehicles available ways to record structures and control illegal construction.
issues.conclusion: Municipal corporations in the State with populations of at least 50 lakhs must geomap and geo-photograph their jurisdictions and the surrounding area extending 10 kilometres from their boundaries, and complete the initial exercise within one year. When an unmapped area is added to a municipality, the corporation must arrange for its geomapping at the earliest; the State must ensure sufficient funding.
issues.legal_principle: The court issued directions using available geographic information technology to improve evidence about the existence, dimensions, and nature of buildings and to assist municipal enforcement against illegal construction.

predicates.municipal_governance_proceeding: The matter concerns the duties of a municipal corporation in administering and documenting its area.
predicates.large_municipal_corporation: The municipal corporation is in the State and serves a population of at least 50 lakhs.

issues.definition: A large municipal corporation in the State must use geomapping and geo-photography to document its area.

issues.legal_issue: Plans and three-dimensional visual records of an existing structure must be provided before construction, reconstruction, or non-tenantable repairs while the State has not legislated on the matter.
material_facts: Some existing buildings had no sanctioned plans, making it difficult to determine whether work amounted to tenantable repairs or required permission.
The court found that recording the existing structure before work would make its dimensions ascertainable even if a later demolition were unlawful.
issues.conclusion: Until the State frames legislation on the matter, the owner, occupier, builder, contractor, and architect must provide a plan of the existing structure and three-dimensional visual information, such as photographs or videos, before construction, reconstruction, or repairs that are not tenantable repairs.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 342 and 347 of the Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act require notice and permission for specified additions, alterations, and repairs, while tenantable repairs are a defined exception. To preserve reliable evidence of existing structures where plans may be unavailable, the court directed that plans and visual records be furnished before the relevant work begins, pending State legislation.

predicates.construction_or_reconstruction_or_non_te: An owner, occupier, builder, contractor, or architect proposes construction, reconstruction, or a repair that is not a tenantable repair.
predicates.no_state_law_on_existing_structure_recor: The State has not enacted legislation governing the provision of records of the existing structure before such work.

issues.definition: When such work is proposed and no State legislation governs the records, plans and visual records of the existing structure must be provided first.

issues.legal_issue: Municipal authorities must use documented evidence, reasoned decisions, and appropriate notice procedures when acting against alleged illegal existing buildings or ongoing construction.
material_facts: The court identified disputes over the existence, dimensions, and nature of alleged illegal structures and disputes about service of notices.
The court directed the use of dated digital photographs and visual images, reasoned decisions on replies, and service by personal and electronic means where appropriate.
issues.conclusion: For alleged illegal existing buildings, authorities must provide dated visual evidence with the show-cause notice, consider any reply and give a reasoned order, and provide further notice before demolition if the reply is unsatisfactory. For ongoing illegal construction, authorities must use the shorter show-cause process, may issue a stop-construction order supported by dated images, and must provide a reasoned decision and further notice before demolition if the reply is unsatisfactory. Notices may be served personally and electronically, and the notice must provide contact details for replies.
issues.legal_principle: Section 351 of the Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act supplies the statutory show-cause and removal framework. The court supplemented its application with procedures intended to provide reliable evidence, fair consideration of replies, effective notice, and an opportunity to approach an appellate or revisional authority or the High Court before demolition.

predicates.municipal_illegal_construction_enforceme: A municipal authority is taking enforcement action against an alleged violation of building requirements.
predicates.alleged_existing_or_ongoing_illegal_cons: The alleged violation concerns either a building already in existence or construction currently in progress.

issues.definition: When a municipality enforces building requirements against an existing or ongoing alleged violation, it must follow the prescribed evidence and notice process.
